Parent with asthma, especially the mother

Occupational exposure to chemical irritants or industrial dusts

Allergic rhinitis or eczema in the family

chief_complaints.text: I keep wheezing and I can't catch my breath
I've been coughing at night for weeks
I get winded when I run or climb stairs

hpi.onset: Episodic symptoms that come and go over months to years; a single flare can build over hours to days
hpi.duration: Symptoms are recurrent; each episode lasts hours to days and often resolves with treatment
hpi.progression: Symptoms wax and wane with triggers; between episodes the patient may feel completely normal
hpi.location: Chest, felt as tightness or a band around the chest
hpi.quality: Whistling or wheezing breath, chest tightness, and a dry hacking cough
hpi.severity: Mild to severe; during a flare the patient may only speak in short phrases and feel air-hungry
hpi.timing: Often worse at night and in the early morning; worse with exercise, cold air or allergen exposure
aggravating: Exercise, especially in cold dry air
Dust, pollen, mold or pet dander
Aspirin or NSAIDs in a sensitive patient
relieving: Inhaled albuterol or another rescue inhaler
Inhaled or oral corticosteroids during a flare

associated_symptoms.text: Itchy watery eyes and sneezing with allergen exposure
Waking at night from cough or wheeze
Difficulty completing sentences or feeding during a severe flare

pertinent_negatives: Fever with chills and productive purulent sputum
Pleuritic chest pain that worsens with deep breaths
Unilateral leg swelling or calf pain
Symptoms that started after starting a new medication such as an ACE inhibitor
Occupational exposure with symptoms only at work and improvement on weekends

negatives: Unilateral facial pain with purulent discharge
Chest pain with exertion that resolves with rest
Urticaria with swelling of lips or tongue

positives.text: Known allergies to dust, pollen, pets or mold
Seasonal worsening in spring or fall

atypical.how_it_differs: Young children may not wheeze audibly; they present with recurrent cough, night waking, poor feeding, or exercise limitation. Parents may describe noisy breathing or a chronic 'chesty' cough.
Symptoms may be attributed to aging or COPD; cough and dyspnea on exertion predominate and wheezing may be absent. Spirometry is needed to separate asthma from COPD and heart failure.
Symptoms can improve, worsen, or stay the same; dyspnea of pregnancy and reflux cough can mimic asthma, and objective testing is needed before changing therapy.
Dyspnea and exercise limitation are common from deconditioning and weight, so symptoms may be blamed on weight rather than asthma; spirometry is essential.

general.mild: Comfortable, speaking in full sentences, no distress
general.moderate: Mildly distressed, speaking in full sentences but pausing, prefers sitting upright
general.severe: Distressed, speaking in short phrases, sitting upright and leaning forward, using accessory muscles
general.critical: Exhausted or drowsy, speaking in single words or unable to speak, tripod position, may be diaphoretic

labs.caveat: A modest eosinophilia supports an allergic (atopic) phenotype but is neither sensitive nor specific; a normal value does not argue against asthma.
Usually normal in asthma; a marked rise should prompt consideration of pneumonia or another infection.
Normal in asthma; helps exclude bacterial pneumonia when fever or purulent sputum is present.
Measured on arterial blood gas. Early in a severe flare the PaCO2 is low from hyperventilation; a normal or rising PaCO2 in a distressed patient signals impending respiratory failure.
Measured on arterial blood gas; hypoxemia worsens with severity.
Respiratory alkalosis early; a falling pH with a rising PaCO2 indicates a life-threatening flare.
Low bicarbonate with a rising PaCO2 suggests a prolonged severe flare with metabolic compensation.
Order in anyone who could be pregnant before imaging or systemic corticosteroids.

Peaked P waves in lead II (P pulmonale)

Assess severity and control at every visit to guide treatment step-up or step-down

criteria.name: Asthma diagnosis
criteria.summary: A history of recurrent wheeze, cough, chest tightness, or dyspnea that varies over time and with triggers, plus objective evidence of variable expiratory airflow limitation (reduced FEV1/FVC that improves after a bronchodilator, or documented variability in peak flow or bronchial challenge testing).
items: Recurrent episodes of wheeze, cough, chest tightness, or dyspnea
Symptoms worse at night or early morning
Symptoms triggered by exercise, allergens, cold air, or viral infections
Objective demonstration of reversible or variable airflow obstruction

differential.name: Vocal cord dysfunction
differential.why_considered: Paroxysmal dyspnea and noisy breathing that can mimic an asthma flare, often in younger patients with anxiety or high-level athletes

history: Symptoms come on and stop abruptly, often within minutes
Nocturnal symptoms are uncommon
Symptoms are triggered by talking, singing, exercise, or strong odors rather than typical allergens
Poor response to inhaled bronchodilators and corticosteroids
exam: Wheeze is loudest over the neck or larynx rather than the chest
Voice change or hoarseness during an episode
Wheeze does not change with position or deep breathing
labs: Normal pulse oximetry during a severe-appearing episode
imaging: Flow-volume loop shows inspiratory flattening rather than the expiratory flattening of asthma
Laryngoscopy during symptoms shows paradoxical vocal cord adduction

differential.name: Foreign body aspiration
differential.why_considered: Sudden onset of cough, wheeze, or dyspnea, especially in a toddler who cannot describe a choking event
differential.trigger: Abrupt onset of symptoms in a child or any patient with a choking episode, unilateral wheeze, or asymmetric breath sounds

history: Sudden onset while eating or playing
Choking or gagging episode reported by a caregiver
Symptoms do not respond to bronchodilators
No prior history of recurrent wheeze
exam: Unilateral wheeze or decreased breath sounds
Focal findings that do not shift with coughing
imaging: Chest x-ray may show hyperinflation, atelectasis, or a radiopaque object on the affected side
Air trapping on expiratory films or CT

differential.name: Bronchiolitis
differential.why_considered: Wheeze, cough, and increased work of breathing in an infant or toddler during viral season

history: First episode in a child under 2 years
Preceded by 1-3 days of rhinorrhea and low-grade fever
Occurs during fall or winter viral season
No prior recurrent episodes or atopic history
exam: Tachypnea and retractions proportionate to illness
labs: Viral testing positive for RSV or another respiratory virus
imaging: Chest x-ray shows hyperinflation with perihilar infiltrates or atelectasis

differential.name: Gastroesophageal reflux disease
differential.why_considered: Chronic nocturnal cough and chest discomfort that can be mistaken for asthma, and reflux is a common comorbidity that worsens asthma control

history: Cough and chest burning worse after meals or when lying flat
Sour taste or regurgitation
No clear response to asthma controller therapy
Symptoms improve with acid suppression
labs: Spirometry is normal without reversible obstruction
imaging: Ambulatory pH monitoring shows pathologic acid exposure

differential.name: Heart failure
differential.why_considered: Dyspnea, wheeze, and exercise limitation in an older adult can be mistaken for late-onset asthma
differential.trigger: Dyspnea with orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, leg swelling, or an elevated jugular venous pressure in an older adult

history: Progressive dyspnea over weeks rather than episodic flares
Orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea
Leg swelling
Known coronary disease, hypertension, or valve disease
imaging: Chest x-ray shows cardiomegaly, pulmonary venous congestion, or pleural effusions
Echocardiogram shows reduced ejection fraction or diastolic dysfunction

differential.name: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
differential.why_considered: Chronic dyspnea, cough, and wheeze with airflow obstruction in an adult, especially a smoker

history: Long-standing daily productive cough
Substantial tobacco or occupational exposure history
Symptoms are persistent and progressive rather than episodic
Onset usually after age 40
exam: Barrel chest with decreased breath sounds
Prolonged expiration that does not fully reverse with bronchodilators
labs: Spirometry shows obstruction with incomplete or no bronchodilator reversibility
imaging: Chest x-ray shows hyperinflation, flattened diaphragms, and increased retrosternal air space

differential.name: Pneumonia
differential.why_considered: Cough, dyspnea, and wheeze during an acute flare, especially when fever or purulent sputum is present

history: Acute onset over hours to a few days with fever and chills
Productive cough with purulent sputum
Pleuritic chest pain
exam: Focal crackles, bronchial breath sounds, egophony, or dullness to percussion
imaging: Chest x-ray shows focal consolidation or infiltrate

differential.name: Pulmonary embolism
differential.why_considered: Acute dyspnea and chest discomfort that can be mistaken for an asthma flare
differential.trigger: Sudden dyspnea with pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, unilateral leg swelling, or risk factors such as recent surgery, immobility, or prior VTE

history: Abrupt onset of dyspnea without a typical trigger
Pleuritic chest pain
Recent surgery, immobility, long travel, or prior clot
Unilateral leg swelling or calf pain
exam: Tachycardia out of proportion to the lung exam
labs: Hypoxemia with a normal chest x-ray
imaging: CT pulmonary angiography shows filling defects in the pulmonary arteries

differential.name: Anaphylaxis
differential.why_considered: Acute wheeze and dyspnea after an allergen exposure, which can look like a severe asthma flare
differential.trigger: Wheeze with urticaria, angioedema, hypotension, or rapid progression after a food, drug, or sting exposure

history: Exposure to a known or suspected allergen minutes before symptoms
Rapid progression over minutes
Flushing, itching, or throat tightness
exam: Urticaria, angioedema of the lips or tongue
labs: Elevated serum tryptase in some cases

differential.name: Inhaled corticosteroid nonadherence or poor inhaler technique
differential.why_considered: Symptoms that persist despite escalating therapy, which can be mistaken for severe refractory asthma

history: Frequent rescue inhaler use but infrequent controller use
Running out of controller inhalers early or late
Symptoms improve during hospitalization or when observed taking medication
exam: Poor coordination with a metered-dose inhaler
labs: Low or undetectable serum cortisol in some patients on high-dose inhaled steroids

severity.mild: Symptoms less than twice a week, nighttime awakenings less than twice a month, no limitation of activity, FEV1 at or above 80% predicted, and symptoms controlled with as-needed albuterol alone
severity.moderate: Daily symptoms, nighttime awakenings more than once a week, some activity limitation, FEV1 60-79% predicted, and need for daily controller therapy
severity.severe: Symptoms throughout the day, frequent nighttime awakenings, marked activity limitation, FEV1 below 60% predicted, and need for high-dose controller therapy; during a flare the patient speaks in short phrases, uses accessory muscles, and has an oxygen saturation in the high 80s to low 90s
severity.critical: Life-threatening flare with a silent chest, exhaustion, drowsiness, inability to speak, cyanosis, oxygen saturation below 90%, and a normal or rising PaCO2 in a distressed patient indicating impending respiratory failure

red_flags.finding: Silent chest with minimal or absent breath sounds
red_flags.meaning: Airflow is critically low; impending respiratory arrest

red_flags.finding: Normal or rising PaCO2 in a distressed patient
red_flags.meaning: The patient is tiring and heading toward respiratory failure; this is not reassuring

red_flags.finding: Drowsiness, confusion, or inability to speak
red_flags.meaning: Hypoxemia and hypercapnia; needs immediate airway support

red_flags.finding: Cyanosis or oxygen saturation below 90% on room air
Use of accessory muscles, tripod position, or intercostal retractions
Heart rate above 120 or respiratory rate above 30
Poor response to repeated albuterol doses
red_flags.meaning: Refractory bronchospasm; consider systemic corticosteroids and possible admission

red_flags.finding: Peak expiratory flow below 50% of personal best

complications.name: Acute severe asthma flare requiring emergency care
clues: Progressive dyspnea over hours to days

complications.name: Airway remodeling with fixed airflow limitation
clues: Spirometry that no longer fully reverses with bronchodilators

complications.name: Corticosteroid adverse effects
clues: Weight gain, hyperglycemia, osteoporosis, cataracts, or adrenal suppression

complications.name: Sleep disruption and impaired quality of life

special_populations.differences: Young children may not wheeze audibly and instead present with recurrent cough, night waking, poor feeding, or exercise limitation. Spirometry is feasible from about age 5-6; younger children are managed on symptoms and response to a trial of controller therapy. Caregiver education on inhaler technique with a spacer and mask is essential.

Symptoms may be attributed to aging or COPD, and heart failure is a common mimic. Spirometry is needed to separate asthma from COPD and cardiac disease, and comorbidities and polypharmacy increase the risk of drug interactions.

Symptoms can improve, worsen, or stay the same. Uncontrolled asthma is more dangerous to the fetus than controller therapy, so inhaled corticosteroids should be continued. Dyspnea of pregnancy and reflux cough can mimic asthma, so objective testing is needed before changing therapy. Check a pregnancy test before imaging or systemic corticosteroids in anyone who could be pregnant.
Dyspnea and exercise limitation are common from deconditioning and weight, so symptoms may be blamed on weight rather than asthma. Spirometry is essential, and weight loss improves control.
Systemic corticosteroids during flares can cause marked hyperglycemia; monitor glucose closely and adjust diabetes therapy when oral steroids are used.
Not a major modifier of asthma itself, but monitor electrolytes and renal function when systemic corticosteroids or frequent beta-agonists are used.
Infections are a more likely cause of new wheeze and dyspnea; lower the threshold for chest imaging and infectious workup before attributing symptoms to asthma.

key_questions.question: What do your symptoms feel like — wheezing, chest tightness, cough, or shortness of breath?
key_questions.looking_for: Wheeze, chest tightness, dry cough, and dyspnea, often in combination

key_questions.question: Do the symptoms come and go, or are they there all the time?
key_questions.looking_for: Episodic and variable over time, with symptom-free intervals between flares

key_questions.question: What seems to set them off?
key_questions.looking_for: Exercise, cold air, dust, pollen, pets, mold, smoke, strong odors, or viral colds

key_questions.question: Are they worse at night or early in the morning?
key_questions.looking_for: Nocturnal or early-morning worsening, a hallmark of asthma

key_questions.question: How often do symptoms occur, and how many nights a month do they wake you?
key_questions.looking_for: Frequency of daytime symptoms and nighttime awakenings, which grade control and severity

key_questions.question: What makes them better?
key_questions.looking_for: Improvement with a rescue inhaler, rest, or avoiding the trigger

key_questions.question: Do you have a history of allergies, eczema, or hay fever?
key_questions.looking_for: Atopic history supporting an allergic phenotype

key_questions.question: Does anyone in your family have asthma, allergies, or eczema?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of asthma or atopy, especially in a parent

key_questions.question: What inhalers or other medicines do you use, and how often do you actually use them?
key_questions.looking_for: Rescue versus controller inhaler use, frequency, and adherence

key_questions.question: Do you take aspirin, ibuprofen, or naproxen, and do they make your breathing worse?
key_questions.looking_for: NSAID sensitivity suggesting aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease

key_questions.question: Does anyone smoke at home, or do you smoke or vape?
key_questions.looking_for: Tobacco or secondhand smoke exposure, a common trigger and worsening factor

key_questions.question: Are there pets, mold, cockroaches, or mice where you live?
key_questions.looking_for: Indoor allergen exposures that can be reduced

key_questions.question: What kind of work do you do, and are symptoms better on days away from work?
key_questions.looking_for: Occupational exposure with improvement away from work, suggesting occupational asthma

key_questions.question: Have you had fever, chills, or coughed up blood or colored sputum?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent in typical asthma; present suggests pneumonia or another cause

key_questions.question: Have you had sudden chest pain, leg swelling, or a choking episode?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; present raises concern for pneumothorax, pulmonary embolism, or foreign body aspiration

key_questions.question: Have you ever been intubated, admitted, or treated in the emergency department for your breathing?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior severe flares, which predict future risk

key_questions.question: Do you have heartburn, postnasal drip, or nasal congestion?
key_questions.looking_for: Reflux or allergic rhinitis that can worsen control

reasoning_points: Recurrent, episodic wheeze, cough, chest tightness, or dyspnea that varies over time
Symptoms worse at night or early morning and provoked by typical triggers such as exercise, allergens, cold air, or viral infections
Personal or family history of atopy (allergic rhinitis, eczema, food allergy)
Between episodes the patient may feel well and the lung exam may be normal
Objective evidence of variable expiratory airflow limitation, such as a reduced FEV1/FVC ratio that improves after a short-acting bronchodilator on spirometry
Alternative causes of dyspnea and wheeze considered and excluded, including pneumonia, heart failure, COPD, pulmonary embolism, and foreign body aspiration

easy: Child or young adult with a long history of episodic wheeze
Clear trigger pattern and nocturnal worsening
Known atopy or family history of asthma
Diffuse expiratory wheeze on exam and improvement with albuterol
medium: Symptoms mainly with exercise, with a normal exam between episodes
Cough-variant presentation with chronic nocturnal cough and little wheeze
Adult with new symptoms that could be COPD or heart failure
Symptoms during a viral illness that persist after the infection clears
hard: Older adult with dyspnea and wheeze later attributed to heart failure
Toddler with recurrent cough and no audible wheeze
Patient with symptoms that persist despite escalating therapy because of poor inhaler technique or nonadherence
Pregnant patient with dyspnea that could be dyspnea of pregnancy or reflux
Occupational presentation with symptoms only at work
